docs.title: What the system does
docs.text:
• Storefront: browse by car model and part type, check which cars a part fits, save your car in My Garage, add variants to the cart, and pay online (prepaid, or Cash on Delivery with a 15% online advance). Guests can check out without an account.
  • Admin panel: products, variants, fitment, categories, orders and COD collection, promo codes, settings, home page, leads, analytics and an audit log.
  • API: prices every checkout on the server, verifies every PayU payment, and reconciles lost payment callbacks every 15 minutes.

docs.title: Criteria for Project Selection
docs.text: This document defines the criteria we will use to choose projects for our software engineering course. It emphasizes time-to-value through rapid iterations, supported by CI/CD to enable frequent build, test, and delivery. Selection also considers contextual relevance, available engineering engines, scalability, and measurable evaluation criteria to ensure we build solutions that can be validated quickly and effectively.

docs.title: Time-to-value
docs.text:
We shall design for rapid delivery, i.e. deliver meaningful increments within a short time window (say weekly). And, prioritize fast feedback over perfection, in order to reduce waiting time between decisions and results.

Initially, you may think of it as:

  • Ship a usable increment within 2 weeks.
  • Complete discovery + prototype + validation in one 2-week sprint.
  • Success is defined by what can be delivered in the first 2-week iteration.

docs.title: CI/ CD
docs.text:
You might have guessed that the core requirement of this project is to showcase multiple iterations of build, test, and ship, fast enough for user/ client to get quick feedback about the product.

To support our short weekly iteration cadence, we should automate build/test/release as much as practical. CI/CD is a good way to achieve that—starting with the lightest pipeline we can (e.g., CI first) and expanding only if it improves delivery.

docs.title: 1. Relevance
docs.text:
Contextual relevance: The problem affects our immediate stakeholders and is within our current scope to influence.

A rough equivalent of need statement. We shall prefer that your problem be of,

  • Local relevance, i.e, relevance to your local environment/region/team.
  • Immediate applicability, i.e, we can act on it now.
  • (to some extent) Near-term impact, i.e, its outcomes are soon visible.

docs.title: 2. Engine availability
docs.text:
This is an engineering course and not a research course. Hence, a necessary heuristic for selection, should be that one or more mature engine(s) should be available as an engine for the core solution of the problem.

We shall address the issues of scalability and complexity here, rather than fundamental algorithms itself. Intuitively, we’ll focus on administrative aspects of software development, more than operational or creative aspects.

PS: Research delays shall not be entertained.

docs.title: 3. Scalability
docs.text:
With foresight, your project should be scalable in the following contexts:

  1. Scalable: Theoretically speaking, your proposition should in principle scale to a larger audience than intended.
  2. Operationally Deployable: Practically speaking, your proposition should be deployable using the available solutions for an extremely large audience.

docs.title: 4. Evaluation Criterion
docs.text:
Evaluation criterion: How will we know it worked?

A good proposition/solution usually includes a way to judge whether the solution actually works.

The evaluation criterion should be measurable (and ideally attributable).

Examples

  • Problem: “Students can’t find answers fast.” Solution: “Add an FAQ search.” Evaluation criterion: “Search results find the correct answer within 10 seconds, and users report satisfaction ≥ 4/5.”

  • Problem: “The app is slow.” Solution: “Optimize queries.” Evaluation criterion: “Page load time decreases from 3s to under 1.5s in production.”

docs.title: 5. Higher-order goal
docs.text:
Treat this as a secondary heuristic, i.e. something to be fulfilled with a lower priority.

It can be very useful—but mostly as a framing layer, not as the whole engineering plan. A higher-order goal, /e.g./ address climate change, helps

  1. Guides priorities,
  2. Creates measurable outcomes,
  3. Makes the problem-solution link easier to justify.

But we still need to translate that why (climate change) into a measurable problem, e.g.

  • Reduce e-waste and “time-to-replace”
  • Reduce network energy and hardware load
  • Lower lifecycle impact by improving reliability (or durability)
  • Sustainable operations
  • Digital efficiency

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: In selecting a project, we prioritize measurable time-to-value through rapid, incremental delivery and fast feedback. CI/CD is the practical mechanism that makes shipping dependable. We focus on problems with contextual relevance, available engineering engines, and scalable, deployable solutions—validated through clear evaluation criteria—while keeping higher-order goals as supportive framing rather than primary drivers.

docs.title: Key modules
docs.text:
Pricing (lib/pricing.ts): subtotal from current SKU prices in integer paise; free shipping when the pre-discount subtotal reaches the threshold; GST shown as net − net / (1 + rate) because prices are GST-inclusive; total = subtotal − discount + shipping.

Payments (lib/payu.ts, routes/webhooks.ts, lib/mark-paid.ts): the order is created first; the PayU request is signed with SHA-512; the return callback and the webhook both verify the hash and the amount before the order becomes paid. reconcile-pending runs every 15 minutes for lost callbacks.

Authentication (routes/auth.ts, lib/otp.ts): six-digit email OTP, bcrypt-hashed, 5-minute expiry, 5 attempts (counted atomically in SQL), rate limited per email and per IP. Admin tokens use a separate secret and the admin flag is re-checked in the database.

Fitment and My Garage: product_fitments links products to vehicle models; the storefront garageStore keeps the shopper's car and filters search and category results.

docs.title: Business rules
docs.text:
• Prices include GST (default 28%, set by the admin).
  • Shipping is free from the admin-set threshold (default ₹5,000); otherwise a flat fee applies (default ₹200).
  • COD orders pay a 15% advance online; the balance is collected on delivery.
  • Only active products can be ordered.

docs.title: Viva Preparation
docs.text: Short answers to the theory questions the evaluation lists (SDLC, SRS, UML, DFD, testing), each tied back to this project. Every member should be able to answer all of these, including the project-specific questions at the end.

docs.title: SDLC models
docs.text:
What is the SDLC? The stages software goes through: requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment and maintenance.

Model Idea When it fits Waterfall One phase after another, no going back Fixed, well-understood requirements V-model Waterfall where each phase has a matching test level (requirements ↔ acceptance test, design ↔ integration test, code ↔ unit test) Safety-critical systems Incremental Build the system in usable slices Early value, stable core Iterative Repeat design → build → review to refine Requirements learnt along the way Spiral Iterations driven by risk analysis Large, high-risk projects Prototype Build a throwaway model to clarify requirements Unclear UI or requirements Agile (Scrum) Short sprints, working software each sprint, continuous feedback Changing requirements, small teams

Which model did we use and why? Iterative and incremental with weekly slices (Agile-style). Payment-gateway behaviour, hosting limits and search ranking could only be learnt by shipping, so Waterfall would have locked in wrong assumptions. Each slice went through a pull request and CI before deployment.

docs.title: SRS
docs.text:
What is an SRS? A document that states what the system must do, not how: functional requirements, non-functional requirements, constraints, interfaces and assumptions. It is the contract between client and developers and the basis for test cases.

Standard? IEEE 830 (now ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148). Ours follows its structure: Introduction → Overall Description → System Features → Non-functional Requirements → Other Requirements.

Functional vs non-functional? Functional = a behaviour ("the system shall verify the PayU hash before marking an order paid", FR-PAY-02). Non-functional = a quality or constraint ("a cached page shall respond in under 300 ms", NFR-PER-01).

Qualities of a good SRS? Correct, unambiguous, complete, consistent, verifiable (testable), modifiable, traceable (every requirement has an ID, e.g. FR-CAT-01).

Requirement elicitation techniques? Interviews (with the store owner), observation (of how orders were handled), analysing the existing system (the old hosted store), questionnaires, prototyping.

docs.title: UML
docs.text:
Structural diagrams: class, object, component, deployment, package. Behavioural diagrams: use case, sequence, activity, state machine, communication.

Use case diagram: actors (Customer, Admin, PayU) and their goals. - include: always part of the base use case (checkout includes payment). - extend: optional, conditional behaviour (apply promo code extends checkout). - generalisation: Customer inherits everything a Guest can do.

Class diagram relationships: - Association: Product — VehicleModel (fits). - Association class: Fitment, data about the Product–VehicleModel link. - Composition (filled diamond): Order ◆— OrderItem; items cannot exist without the order. - Aggregation (hollow diamond): a whole–part link where parts can live alone. - Generalisation (hollow triangle): inheritance. - Multiplicity: 1, 0..1, 0..*, 1..* on each end.

Sequence diagram: objects over time with messages; we drew checkout: UI → API → DB → PayU → API verifies → mark paid → Inngest. opt = optional fragment, alt = if/else, loop = repetition.

Activity diagram: workflow with actions, decisions (diamonds), forks/joins and swimlanes (Customer | Application | PayU).

State machine diagram: states of one object and the events that move it. Our order: pending → paid → confirmed → shipped → delivered, with cancelled and refunded.

docs.title: DFD
docs.text:
What is a DFD? It shows how data moves through a system: external entities (rectangles), processes (circles), data stores (open rectangles) and data flows (arrows). It shows data, not control or timing.

Levels: Level 0 (context diagram) = the whole system as one process with its external entities. Level 1 = the main processes (ours: 1.0 Browse and cart, 2.0 Checkout and payment, 3.0 Order management) with data stores D1 Catalogue, D2 Orders, D3 Settings. Level 2 breaks a Level-1 process down further.

Rules: every process has at least one input and one output; data cannot flow directly between two stores or two external entities; levels must be balanced (same inputs/outputs at parent and child level).

DFD vs flowchart? A DFD shows data movement; a flowchart shows control flow and decisions.

docs.title: ER diagram
docs.text: Entities (Product, Order), attributes, relationships with cardinality (1:1, 1:N, M:N). M:N is implemented with a junction table: Product–Category uses product_categories.

docs.title: Software testing
docs.text:
Levels: unit → integration → system → acceptance. Black-box: test inputs/outputs without looking at code (equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis). Example boundary: free shipping exactly at ₹5,000 qualifies (>=), ₹4,999 does not. White-box: test using the code's structure (statement, branch, path coverage). Regression testing: re-run tests after every change; our CI does this on every pull request. Alpha/beta testing: alpha in-house, beta with real users. Verification vs validation: verification = "are we building the product right?" (reviews, tests against the spec); validation = "are we building the right product?" (does it meet the user's need). Test case parts: ID, requirement traced, preconditions, steps, input data, expected result, actual result, status. Mocking: replacing a real dependency with a fake one (we use MSW for the API in storefront tests, and test doubles for the DB and PayU in API tests).

Our numbers: 884 automated tests passing (398 API + 486 storefront), run with Vitest in GitHub Actions.

docs.title: Other common questions
docs.text:
• Coupling and cohesion: aim for low coupling between modules and high cohesion inside one. Our API keeps business logic in lib/ and HTTP handling in routes/.
  • CI/CD: continuous integration builds and tests every change; continuous delivery/deployment ships it. Vercel deploys the storefront from main.
  • Software maintenance types: corrective (bug fixes), adaptive (new environment), perfective (improvements), preventive.
  • COCOMO: effort estimation from lines of code (organic, semi-detached, embedded modes).
  • Cyclomatic complexity: number of independent paths = E − N + 2P.

docs.title: Project-specific questions
docs.text:
1. What problem does the project solve? Customers cannot tell whether a part fits their car, and the old hosted store gave no control over search, checkout or payments.
  2. Architecture? Next.js storefront + admin on Vercel, Hono REST API on Fly.io, PostgreSQL and storage on Supabase, PayU for payments.
  3. How do you stop price tampering? The server reloads SKU prices from the database at checkout and ignores any total sent by the browser.
  4. How do you know a payment is real? PayU's response hash (SHA-512) and the amount are verified on the server, on both the return callback and the webhook.
  5. What if the callback never arrives? A background job checks pending orders with PayU every 15 minutes.
  6. How does login work? Six-digit email OTP, stored as a bcrypt hash, valid 5 minutes, 5 attempts, rate-limited.
  7. How is COD handled? 15% advance paid online; the admin marks the balance as collected on delivery.
  8. How is fitment modelled? A product_fitments table between products and vehicle models (many-to-many).
  9. How many tables? 28.
  10. What did you measure? 884 passing tests; Lighthouse SEO 100; cached pages 375–437 ms; mobile LCP not yet within the 2.5 s target.
  11. Biggest challenges? Third-party cookies (fixed with a same-origin proxy), Vercel image quota (moved to Supabase image rendering), a database connectivity outage (moved to the Supabase session pooler).
  12. Future work? Reviews, courier integration, page-speed improvements, Android app.

docs.title: Week 1 : Menu button pushed off-screen on phones
docs.text: Team focus this week: Requirements and project setup Work this week: Storefront header and theme

docs.title: Error
docs.text: On small phones the hamburger menu overflowed off the screen; in dark mode the menu text was invisible.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Header had a large logo, wide icon padding and a theme toggle on every size.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Too many fixed-width items for a 360 px header; the drawer had a white background that dark mode did not override.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Smaller logo and icon padding on mobile, theme toggle hidden below sm, and a .dark override for the drawer background.

Because design phone layout first, then add items for larger screens.

docs.title: Week 2 : Save button cut off on phones
docs.text: Team focus this week: Catalogue and admin panel Work this week: Admin product editor on mobile

docs.title: Error
docs.text: In the admin product editor on a phone, the Save button was off-screen.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Four action buttons with large padding in one row.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: The row was wider than a phone screen.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Reordered to Delete · Cancel · Save · Archive with smaller padding so all four fit.

Because primary actions must stay visible at the smallest screen width.

docs.title: Week 3 : Shop menu closed before links could be clicked
docs.text: Team focus this week: Login and accounts Work this week: Shop mega-menu

docs.title: Error

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The menu closed on mouseleave.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: A small gap between button and panel fired mouseleave.

docs.title: Solution

Added a 160 ms close delay, cancelled on re-enter.

Because hover menus need a short grace period to cross gaps.

docs.text: Clicking a subcategory chip sometimes opened the parent category.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: A full-card link was stretched underneath the chips.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Overlapping links: the click could resolve to the link behind.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Restructured so the photo, title and each chip are separate links; all 31 menu links checked.

Because interactive elements should never overlap.

docs.title: Week 5 : Product descriptions lost their formatting
docs.text: Team focus this week: Payments and COD Work this week: Product detail page

docs.title: Error
docs.text: Descriptions with "Key Features" and "Specifications" showed as one paragraph.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Imported descriptions contain newlines.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: HTML collapses whitespace by default.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Rendered descriptions with whitespace-pre-line.

Because cSS decides how whitespace in text is shown.

docs.title: Week 6 : Product images stopped loading
docs.text: Team focus this week: SEO, images and performance Work this week: Image loading through Supabase

docs.title: Error
docs.text: Product and category images failed on the live site.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Images were resized by Vercel's image optimiser.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: The free monthly optimisation quota was used up.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
A custom image loader uses Supabase's image rendering endpoint.

Because resizing where the images are stored removes a second quota.

docs.title: Week 7 : Guest order could not be placed after autofill
docs.text: Team focus this week: Security and guest checkout Work this week: Guest checkout form

docs.title: Error
docs.text: On a phone, browser autofill broke the mobile number and the order could never be placed.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The input had maxLength=10.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Autofill inserts "+91 98765 43210", which was cut to "+91 98765 ".

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Input accepts any length; toMobile10() strips +91, 91, 0 and spaces. City/state filled from the PIN also clear their errors.

Because validate after normalising input, not by limiting what can be typed.

docs.title: Week 8 : Phone layout wider than the screen
docs.text: Team focus this week: Testing, fixes and launch Work this week: Mobile fixes and design refresh

docs.title: Error
docs.text: The home page was 657 px wide on a 390 px phone.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The hero used a two-column grid with long text.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Grid children default to min-width: auto and refuse to shrink.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
One column on phones, min-w-0 on grid children, break-words.

Because min-width: 0 lets grid and flex items shrink.

docs.title: Week 1 : Product names could inject a script
docs.text: Team focus this week: Requirements and project setup Work this week: SRS draft; security review of structured data

docs.title: Error
docs.text: Security review: a product name containing </script> would break out of the JSON-LD block.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Structured data is printed inside a <script type="application/ld+json"> tag.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Any </script> inside the JSON ends the tag early, allowing stored XSS.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Escape </script> (and <) when writing JSON-LD; covered by tests.

Because data placed inside HTML must be escaped for that context.

docs.title: Week 2 : Pages blank for search engines
docs.text: Team focus this week: Catalogue and admin panel Work this week: Server-rendered pages for search engines

docs.title: Error
docs.text: With JavaScript off, the home page showed grey placeholders and product pages were empty skeletons.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Data sections were wrapped in <Suspense>.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: React streams Suspense content and uses a script to swap it in; without JS the swap never happens.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Removed those boundaries so the server sends finished HTML; checked in a headless browser with JS off (48 product links rendered).

Because crawlers must get complete HTML without running scripts.

docs.title: Week 3 : Duplicate products competing in search
docs.text: Team focus this week: Login and accounts Work this week: Duplicate product URLs

docs.title: Error
docs.text: Three products existed twice in the catalogue and competed for the same searches.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Each copy had its own URL in the sitemap and feed.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Google treats them as duplicate content.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
lib/duplicate-products.ts maps copies to the primary: canonical points to the primary, copies are noindex and left out of sitemap and feed.

Because one canonical URL per product concentrates ranking.

docs.title: Week 4 : Merchant Center feed items at risk of rejection
docs.text: Team focus this week: Vehicle fitment and navigation Work this week: Google Merchant Center feed

docs.title: Error
docs.text: Some feed items would break Google Merchant Center policies.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The feed listed every product with its raw title.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Titles naming third-party brands or "OEM/original" claims risk policy strikes; XML control characters break the feed.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Feed built by a tested lib/merchant-feed.ts: sale price, Google category ids, safe titles, illegal characters stripped; 95 items listed, 27 held back with reasons.

Because only list what the business can confirm.

docs.title: Week 5 : Security advisories in Next.js
docs.text: Team focus this week: Payments and COD Work this week: Dependency security upgrade

docs.title: Error
docs.text: npm audit reported critical advisories in Next.js 16.0.0–16.4.0.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The storefront ran Next.js 16.4.0.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Advisories included remote code execution in the image optimiser.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Upgraded to 16.4.2; type-check, tests and both builds passed, and the mock purchase journey passed 113/113.

Because dependencies need regular security updates.

docs.title: Week 6 : Price shown differed from price charged
docs.text: Team focus this week: SEO, images and performance Work this week: Price-check testing

docs.title: Error
docs.text: Testing found that a guest cart could be charged today's price while showing an older one.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Browser cart lines keep the price from when they were added.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Once SKU ids survived admin edits, old lines still pointed at valid SKUs with new prices.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
New /cart/price-check; cart and checkout re-price every line on load, and Pay is blocked if the order total differs from the shown total.

Because what the customer sees must equal what they are charged.

docs.title: Week 7 : npm ci failed in CI on Linux
docs.text: Team focus this week: Security and guest checkout Work this week: CI workflows

docs.title: Error
docs.text: CI failed: package.json and package-lock.json were not in sync.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The lockfile was generated with legacy-peer-deps=true.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: That setting leaves optional peer dependencies out; a clean Linux install expects them.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Project .npmrc with legacy-peer-deps=false and a regenerated lockfile.

Because a lockfile is reproducible only with the same npm settings everywhere.

docs.title: Week 8 : Search and login pages claimed to be the home page
docs.text: Team focus this week: Testing, fixes and launch Work this week: Canonical URL test; final reports and docs

docs.title: Error
docs.text: Search Console treated search, login and 404 pages as duplicates of the home page.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The root layout set canonical: "/", inherited by every page without its own.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: An inherited canonical told Google each page was a copy of /.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Home sets its own canonical; the layout sets none; a test fails if this regresses.

Because next.js layout metadata is inherited by child pages.

docs.title: Week 1 : Customers could not receive SMS OTPs
docs.text: Team focus this week: Requirements and project setup Work this week: Email-OTP login (switched from SMS)

docs.title: Error
docs.text: The first login sent OTPs by SMS, which needed a registered SMS template before it could go live.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Auth routes, contracts, frontend pages and tests all assumed phone numbers.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Email delivery (Resend) needed no approval and was cheaper.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Migration 0009 adds email auth; routes, contracts, pages, mocks and tests switched from phone to email OTP. SMS is kept only for order updates.

Because choosing a channel the business can actually use unblocks launch.

docs.title: Week 2 : A product could appear in only one category
docs.text: Team focus this week: Catalogue and admin panel Work this week: Multi-category catalogue (junction table)

docs.title: Error
docs.text: The same spoiler had to be listed under both "Spoilers" and "VW Parts".

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: products had a single category_id.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: This is a many-to-many relationship.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Added the product_categories junction table; category listings match any of a product's categories; the admin editor got an "Also list under" field.

Because many-to-many relationships need a junction table.

docs.title: Week 3 : Modelling which car a part fits
docs.text: Team focus this week: Login and accounts Work this week: Vehicle fitment schema and API

docs.title: Error
docs.text: Customers could not tell whether a part fits their car.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Fitment data existed only as text in descriptions.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Fitment belongs to the pair (product, vehicle model), not to either one.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Migration for vehicle_makes, vehicle_models and product_fitments, /vehicles routes and Zod contracts; used by the garage selector and the admin fitment editor.

Because an association table stores facts about a relationship.

docs.title: Week 4 : Header menu stayed stale after admin edits
docs.text: Team focus this week: Vehicle fitment and navigation Work this week: Category caching and invalidation

docs.title: Error
docs.text: Changing which categories show in the header had no effect until the cache expired.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Cache invalidation cleared keys starting with category:.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: The header reads the key categories:all, which that prefix does not match.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Added categories:all to the invalidation explicitly; the frontend now revalidates the SWR key the header really uses (shop-nav).

Because cache invalidation must name every key that holds the data.

docs.title: Week 5 : Rate limits could be bypassed
docs.text: Team focus this week: Payments and COD Work this week: Rate limiting for OTP and login

docs.title: Error
docs.text: An attacker could get a fresh OTP and login budget on every request.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Rate-limit keys used the leftmost X-Forwarded-For address.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: The client sets that header itself, so it can rotate it at will.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Keys now use Fly-Client-IP, then X-Real-IP, and only then the last X-Forwarded-For hop (added by our proxy).

Because only trust headers your own infrastructure sets.

docs.title: Week 6 : Session lost on Safari and Firefox
docs.text: Team focus this week: SEO, images and performance Work this week: Session cookies via same-origin proxy

docs.title: Error
docs.text: Safari and Firefox users were logged out after about 15 minutes.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The refresh cookie came from the API's domain, different from the storefront's.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: For the storefront that is a third-party cookie, which these browsers block.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
All session calls go through a same-origin Next.js proxy, so the cookie is first-party.

Because a cookie is first-party only for the site in the address bar.

docs.title: Week 7 : OTP attempt limit could be bypassed
docs.text: Team focus this week: Security and guest checkout Work this week: Security hardening (OTP attempts)

docs.title: Error
docs.text: Many simultaneous guesses got more than the 5 permitted attempts.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Each guess read attempts, checked it, then wrote attempts + 1.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Read-then-write race: concurrent requests all read the same old value.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
One atomic UPDATE otp_codes SET attempts = attempts + 1 WHERE id = $1 AND attempts < 5 RETURNING id; no row means 429.

Because a single conditional UPDATE is atomic in PostgreSQL.

docs.title: Week 8 : Editing a price emptied customers' carts
docs.text: Team focus this week: Testing, fixes and launch Work this week: Admin product API (SKU sync)

docs.title: Error
docs.text: After an admin saved a product, carts containing it became empty.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: PATCH /admin/products/:id deleted every SKU row and inserted new ones.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: cart_items.sku_id cascades on delete, so every save wiped those cart lines.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
SKUs are now synced in place: matched by id then code, updated; only removed SKUs are deleted.

Because updating rows keeps their ids, so references to them survive.

docs.title: Week 1 : Choosing and wiring the payment gateway
docs.text: Team focus this week: Requirements and project setup Work this week: PayU integration; deployment setup (Vercel, Fly.io, Supabase)

docs.title: Error
docs.text: The store needed online payments; the first integration used Razorpay, which the business would not use.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Checkout code called one provider directly.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Payments needed to be swappable without touching checkout logic.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Added a provider selector (lib/payments.ts) and a PayU hosted-checkout module (lib/payu.ts) with request/response hashing, a browser return route and a server webhook, plus PayU columns on orders (migration 0011). Razorpay was switched off.

Because hiding the provider behind one interface keeps checkout independent of the gateway.

docs.title: Week 2 : Launch build never deployed on Vercel
docs.text: Team focus this week: Catalogue and admin panel Work this week: Fixed the storefront deployment pipeline

docs.title: Error
docs.text: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile failed on Vercel and the launch build did not go live.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: svcar-india uses npm (package-lock.json), but a stray, outdated pnpm-lock.yaml had been committed.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Vercel picks the package manager from the lockfile it finds; it chose pnpm and the pnpm lockfile was out of date.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Deleted the stray pnpm-lock.yaml, so Vercel used the in-sync package-lock.json and npm ci passed.

Because a project must have exactly one lockfile for one package manager.

docs.title: Week 3 : Customer signed out after paying
docs.text: Team focus this week: Login and accounts Work this week: Order confirmation page after payment

docs.title: Error
docs.text: After paying on PayU the customer came back logged out and landed on the login page.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The refresh cookie was SameSite=Lax, and PayU redirected to /orders/:n, which needs login.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: The storefront and the API are different sites, so a Lax cookie is not sent on cross-site refresh calls; the PayU return is a full page load, so the session was lost.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Refresh cookie set to SameSite=None; Secure in production; PayU now returns to a public /order-confirmation/:n page with the order number, a Track button and Retry on failure.

Because cross-site requests only carry cookies marked SameSite=None; Secure.

docs.title: Week 4 : COD advance not enforced at the gateway
docs.text: Team focus this week: Vehicle fitment and navigation Work this week: COD advance amount in the API

docs.title: Error
docs.text: A COD order could be sent to PayU with a stored amount instead of the 15% advance.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The webhook and checkout each worked out the advance in their own way.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: There was no single function for "how much goes to PayU".

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Added gatewayPaymentAmount(total, method) in lib/payment-amount.ts (15% for COD, 100% prepaid, in paise) and used it in checkout and webhook; tests in payment-amount, checkout and webhooks.

Because one shared function means checkout and verification can never disagree.

docs.title: Week 5 : COD advance shown as ₹2.00 instead of ₹1.50
docs.text: Team focus this week: Payments and COD Work this week: COD amounts in the checkout UI

docs.title: Error
docs.text: The checkout button showed a different advance from what PayU charged.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The page computed Math.round(total * 15) / 100.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Rounding before dividing by 100 rounds to whole rupees; the API rounds in paise.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Changed to Math.round(total * 100 * 0.15) / 100, matching the backend.

Because money must be rounded at the same unit (paise) everywhere.

docs.title: Week 6 : Paid amount not compared with order total
docs.text: Team focus this week: SEO, images and performance Work this week: Payment amount checks on return and webhook

docs.title: Error
docs.text: Audit finding: the server trusted the hash alone before marking an order paid.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The reverse hash covers the amount, so this mattered only if the merchant salt ever leaked.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: That is exactly the case the amount check protects against, and PayU requires it.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Both the return URL and the webhook compare the paid amount with the order total; a mismatch keeps the order pending, is logged and alerts the team.

Because defence in depth: a second check catches what the first misses.

docs.title: Week 7 : A retried payment could charge twice
docs.text: Team focus this week: Security and guest checkout Work this week: Payment audit (retry safety)

docs.title: Error
docs.text: If the first attempt succeeded but both callbacks were lost, Retry started a second, real charge.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Retry created a new PayU transaction for the same order without asking PayU about earlier ones.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: PayU, not the browser, knows whether money was taken.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Before a retry the API calls PayU verify_payment for earlier attempts; if one succeeded the order is marked paid and the retry refused with 409. Retry transaction ids are now unique.

Because the gateway is the source of truth for payments.

docs.title: Week 8 : Store went offline — database connection refused
docs.text: Team focus this week: Testing, fixes and launch Work this week: Launch support (database outage)

docs.title: Error
docs.text: Admin login failed and pages were empty; logs showed ECONNREFUSED to an IPv6 address on port 5432.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: DATABASE_URL used Supabase's direct host, which resolves to IPv6.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: The API host could not open IPv6 connections.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Switched to Supabase's session pooler (IPv4) and restarted the API; re-saved home, products and categories to refresh cached pages.

Because the pooler gives an IPv4 endpoint that every host supports.
